source: Pennington and Hastie (1993) The story model for juror decision making, ch. 8 in Hastie (ed.) Inside the Juror (text of Table 8.1)
finding: Order-of-evidence experiment (Pennington and Hastie 1988): 2x2 design, prosecution evidence in story or witness order crossed with defense evidence in story or witness order. Table recovered from the chapter text.
numbers: Percent guilty of murder. Pros story/def story 59; pros story/def witness 78; pros witness/def story 31; pros witness/def witness 63. Row means: pros story 69, pros witness 47. Column means: def story 45, def witness 70. N=130 college students, about 32 per cell (cell sizes not printed). Means check out arithmetically with 63 (not 62).
quote: mock jurors were likeliest to convict the defendant when the prosecution evidence was presented in story order and the defense evidence was presented in witness order (78% chose guilty)
limits: Table layout was garbled by text extraction, but all four cells reconcile with the printed row and column means. No test statistics are given in the chapter. Single case (Commonwealth v. Johnson), audio tape, students. Chapter is a review, not the 1988 journal article.
agent_relevance: Closes the 62 vs 63 question: the both-witness cell is 63. The big swing is when ONE side is easy to build as a story and the other is hard; if both are story-ordered the effect cancels (59). So story order helps whichever side has it.

source: Pennington and Hastie (1993) ch. 8, design and ratings of the order experiment
finding: Details of the 1988 order experiment: 100-item version of the case (50 prosecution, 50 defense statements), tape recorded, prosecution always before defense, verdict, confidence and case-strength ratings collected. Strength ratings and confidence also moved with order.
numbers: N=130. Story-order evidence rated stronger than witness-order evidence. Perceived strength of one side depended on the order of BOTH sides. Confidence was higher when both sides were in story order, whichever verdict was chosen (this was not predicted).
limits: The authors state the study was not built to estimate order effects in real trials; openings, closings, redundancy and visuals that help real jurors build stories were stripped out.
agent_relevance: Supports uniqueness: a strong rival story lowers confidence in the lead story. For our agent: confidence should depend on how well the best rival is built, not only on the lead answer.

source: Pennington and Hastie (1993) ch. 8, fourth study (Pennington and Hastie 1992, story order vs legal-issue order)
finding: Replication and extension with new materials (Devine and Ostrom 1985 cases, two cases, one leaning guilty and one leaning innocent). Evidence in story order versus legal-issue order. Recall clustering followed the order given, but total recall did not differ.
numbers: N=414 college students, written materials. Story-order groups showed high story clustering and low issue clustering in free recall (ARC measure); issue-order groups showed the reverse. Total amount recalled: no difference. Verdicts moved in the expected direction and confidence was higher under story order. Verdict percentages are not printed in the chapter.
limits: Secondary account of the 1992 paper; the JPSP article itself was not opened (paywalled). Effect sizes and test statistics unavailable. Chapter also cites Smith (1988) as a replication with legal-issue order; Smith was not found.
agent_relevance: Rules out the simple reading that order only changes memorability. For the agent: order changes the grouping the model builds, which can be tested while token count and recall stay fixed.

source: Pennington and Hastie (1993) ch. 8, comparisons with Bayesian and anchor-and-adjust models
finding: Two further experiments compared the story model with a Bayesian model and an anchor-and-adjust sequential updating model. Item-by-item ratings fit anchor-and-adjust; global verdict ratings fit neither and fit a story-weight configuration best.
numbers: Global assessments were stronger in force than the final item-by-item rating by a factor of about 1.5. Story-supplement x response-mode interaction on final guilt judgment was obtained. Difference between global ratings and anchor-and-adjust predictions was reliably non-zero; item-by-item differences were not. Sample sizes not printed in the chapter.
limits: Authors' own review of their own studies. Fit comparisons are descriptive. Rival accounts later fit similar data (see b-file and c-file).
agent_relevance: Gap 9 partly: a step-by-step element check behaves like item-by-item updating (additive, less polarised), while one global story judgment is more extreme. Suggests element checks and a global story answer will disagree in strength, not just in threshold.

source: Pennington and Hastie (1993) ch. 8, recognition memory study (Pennington and Hastie 1988) and verdict-learning check
finding: Jurors falsely recognised inferences that belonged to the story of their own verdict, and rated evidence importance by its causal role in that story. Memory of verdict-element definitions was not related to verdict choice.
numbers: Written 119-sentence case. Own-verdict story items accepted at a higher rate than rejected-verdict story items, for both old items and never-presented lures. Exact rates not printed in the chapter. Verdict choice unrelated to memory for verdict-element relations; no content differences by verdict (1986 analyses).
limits: No numbers in the review chapter; primary article not opened.
agent_relevance: Story building inserts unstated inferences that then feel like evidence. Agent risk: a built story will be quoted back as if it were source evidence; keep inferred items tagged separately.

source: Fatemi et al. (2024) Test of Time: a benchmark for evaluating LLMs on temporal reasoning (Table 7, fact order)
finding: Same facts, different order, on the ToT-Semantic set. Shuffled facts gave the lowest accuracy for all three models; sorting by target entity then start time gave the highest for two of three.
numbers: Accuracy (Claude-3-Sonnet / GPT-4 / Gemini 1.5 Pro): Shuffle 45.71 / 60.71 / 63.04; RelationAndStartTime 54.29 / 65.36 / 68.57; StartTimeAndRelation 47.68 / 60.54 / 64.64; StartTimeAndTarget 49.11 / 61.61 / 65.18; TargetAndStartTime 73.57 / 62.60 / 75.00. Shuffle to best: +27.9, +4.6, +12.0 points.
limits: Order by entity and time, not a juror-style causal story; one dataset; no variance reported in the table; GPT-4 gain is small. Token count is the same since the facts are the same. Author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Closest direct LLM answer to gap 2: grouping facts by entity and time order beats shuffled at equal tokens. It does not test causal-story order against source-by-source order; that test still has to be run on our side.

source: Chen et al. (2024) Premise order matters in reasoning with large language models
finding: Reordering the premises of a deductive problem away from the order of the proof (forward order) drops accuracy a lot; forward order is best for every model. Same on rewritten grade-school math (R-GSM).
numbers: Drop up to over 30% on logical tasks; GPT-4-turbo and PaLM 2-L lose up to 20-30% off forward order; Gemini 1.0 Pro and GPT-3.5-turbo go from over 65% to below 25% (drop over 40%) at 12 rules. Gap widens with more rules. R-GSM: 220 problem pairs, models do worse on reordered versions.
limits: Order is the proof order, a logical not narrative order. GPT-4-turbo prefers backward order next; PaLM 2-L is worst on backward. Models are 2023-24 vintage. Text read; the per-condition tables (9-11) were not all read.
agent_relevance: Evidence that order = proof order matters for LLMs, in line with story order. Suggests the scaffold should present facts in the order a solution would use them (causal or proof order) at zero token cost.

source: The SMeL Test: a simple benchmark for media literacy in language models (2025)
finding: Models treat the position of a source differently: Llama models systematically trust earlier sources more, GPT-4o often trusts the last source significantly more, Gemma and o3-mini are largely invariant. Error rates for both orders are non-zero for all models.
numbers: Only the discussion paragraph was read; per-model rates not extracted.
limits: Source credibility test, not story building. Read from extracted text, not every table.
agent_relevance: Order bias in LLMs is model-specific (primacy for Llama, recency for GPT-4o), matching the mixed human and LLM order pattern in the Bessis recency result. Test any order intervention per model.

source: Do Large Language Models (LLMs) Understand Chronology? (2025)
finding: LLMs keep local order but lose a single global timeline as lists grow; reasoning budget fixes it.
numbers: Exact-match rate on ordering lists, GPT-4.1 historical events: n=2 1.00, n=5 0.45, n=10 0.10, n=20 0.00. US presidents (cleaned): n=2 0.96, n=5 0.87, n=10 0.36, n=20 0.10, n>=30 0.00. Claude 3.7 Sonnet with Extended Thinking 1.00 at every size; GPT-5 medium and high effort 1.00 at every size; GPT-5 minimal/no reasoning collapses though rank correlation stays >=0.94.
limits: Only first 100,000 of 161,496 characters read. Ordering lists, not story building.
agent_relevance: Building a clean chronology of many events is itself a failure point without reasoning budget; the story-construction step in our schema should be given thinking budget or be broken into checks.

source: Chhikara (2025) Mind the Confidence Gap: overconfidence, calibration and distractor effects in LLMs
finding: Adding three plausible wrong alternatives next to the correct answer raised accuracy and cut calibration error for most models and datasets, but made calibration worse on an easy dataset for two models.
numbers: 9 models, 3 datasets (SimpleQA 4,326; FaVIQ 2,922; TriviaQA 1,000). SimpleQA GPT-4o: acc 35.14% to 73.42%, ECE 0.450 to 0.037. GPT-4o-mini: acc 8.46% to 47.43%. Mean ECE drop over 27 model-dataset pairs 0.260 (SimpleQA 0.433, FaVIQ 0.292, TriviaQA 0.057). TriviaQA ECE rose for GPT-4-turbo (0.025 to 0.048) and GPT-4o (0.071 to 0.083). Judge GPT-4o-mini kappa 0.82 vs 3 humans (100 items).
limits: Distractors turn open recall into 4-way multiple choice, so the accuracy gain is mostly a format effect. Not rival stories and no coverage or uniqueness scoring. Self-reported 0-100 confidence. Distractors written by GPT-4o-mini. Table read through a fetch summary, not the PDF.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: showing the model rivals helps calibration on hard factual items and can hurt on easy ones (confidence inflation). A rival-story step should be switched on by difficulty, not always.

source: CEDAR-GRPO: process-aware reinforcement learning for general abductive reasoning in LLMs (2026)
finding: Uses an LLM judge to list the atomic details of the observations and check which ones the chosen hypothesis explains (Evidence Coverage), plus a direction-of-reasoning score. Rewarding coverage and direction on top of correctness raised accuracy on held-out reasoning sets, including non-forensic ones (MuSR, StrategyQA, MedQA).
numbers: Coverage on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B averaged over 10 held-out sets: base 33.1%, correctness-only 39.1%, composite 52.9%. Average accuracy ablation: Qwen3-4B composite 52.1 vs 50.3 (coverage only added) and 50.2 (direction only added); R1-Distill-7B 54.1 vs 51.1 and 50.7. Per-task Table 1 numbers were not mapped to columns, so none are quoted.
limits: This is RL training, not prompting. Coverage is judged by an LLM, no entailment check; judge cost/tokens not measured here. Authors rate coverage as resistant to reward hacking only in their own screening table. Not tested as a prompt-time audit.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 and 4 partial: counting how many observation details a hypothesis accounts for transfers to non-forensic tasks and is a trainable signal, which supports using coverage in the scaffold. Prompt-time token cost still unknown.

source: Evidence Integration in Large Language Models (2026)
finding: Models reweight evidence against an already-formed answer distribution: the model's own prior answer is weighted less than 1 (a rational receiver would be 1), and its most common wrong answer works as an attractor.
numbers: 12 instruction-tuned models, more than 10 million trials, 8 domains. Prior weight on arithmetic between 0.20 and 0.65 (SE under 0.02) across 9 models; user channel 0.30-0.85 vs tool channel 0.00-0.44; across 51 model-by-domain cells 0.13-0.69. Paired attractor effect positive in all 9 arithmetic models; Gemma-4-31B +0.590 [+0.520, +0.658], accepts its own modal wrong answer 0.654 vs 0.064 matched controls.
limits: Only the first 100,000 of 324,171 characters read. Arithmetic mostly; small open models. This measures a pull toward the model's own sampled wrong answer, which is related to but not the same as human coherence shift.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: different from coherence shift in human jurors. Open models DISCOUNT their prior (weight below 1) yet are pulled toward a wrong candidate they themselves produce. Early commitment is not simply overweighted; test with a lead answer shown in context.

source: The Challenge of Simulating Human Strategy (2026) - motivated updating in LLMs on Old Bailey trials
finding: LLMs show a pattern in which strong early evidence for one side leads them to discount later contradicting evidence; order of prosecution vs defense changed conviction rates. Fitted parameters for a default LLM in a legal setting reported.
numbers: alpha=1.05, beta=0.38, tau=0.71 (default LLM, legal setting). Models: GPT-5, Claude-3.5-Sonnet prompted; small 7-8B RL-trained models. Data: Old Bailey transcripts 1674-1913. Conviction rate values by order not given in the page; run counts not stated.
limits: Read through an overview page, not the full paper (PDF fetch failed). Numbers are secondary. Historical transcripts rather than story-model manipulations.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 partial: some evidence that LLMs anchor on early evidence in legal evidence streams. Needs the primary paper before use.

source: IRAC-R1: unlocking LLM legal reasoning with IRAC-constrained chain-of-thought (ICML 2026 abstract)
finding: Training a 7B model on IRAC (issue, rule, application, conclusion) structured traces raised Bar Exam QA accuracy.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 47.9% to 58.1% (+10.2 points); 61.5% with gold passages. Authors claim IRAC rather than generic chain-of-thought gives the gain, but no generic-CoT baseline number is on the page. Retrieval named the main bottleneck.
limits: Abstract page only. Fine-tuned with distillation plus RL, not a prompt-only test. Bar exam question answering, not verdict forming. No story-first vs element-first arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and 9: element-by-element structure helps accuracy on legal knowledge QA after training. There is still no test of story-first versus element-first.

source: HypoSpace: evaluating LLM hypothesis sets under underdetermination (2025 abstract)
finding: LLMs keep validity high but lose uniqueness and recovery as hypothesis spaces get larger; stratified decoding reduces the collapse.
numbers: Domains: causal graphs, gravity-constrained voxels, Boolean genetic interactions. Specific figures and model names not on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; no numbers read.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 partial: asking an LLM for several rival stories will return overlapping ones as the space grows. Rival-story prompts need a diversity rule (distinct causal explanations) or they add no uniqueness check.

source: Reardon (FIU dissertation) evidence order and deliberation style with video trials
finding: Search-result summary only: among students, verdict-driven deliberation groups formed more consistent pro-prosecution stories when the prosecution used story order; among community members the pattern reversed.
numbers: No numbers seen. Year about 2009 inferred from the repository id; unverified.
limits: Not opened (page text returned empty). Dissertation, not peer-reviewed. Sample-dependent reversal is a boundary condition but unconfirmed.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the only post-2000 order-of-evidence test found outside the Burd, Curley, Lin and Paterson studies, and it hints at no clean replication in community samples.

source: Search for dated 2000-2026 replications of story vs witness order (Telling Tales in Court, Michigan law review)
finding: Search snippet: a law review notes that the story-order vs witness-order work had not been tested with coherent opening statements.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened; snippet only. Year approximate. Negative-search result: no failed replication of the order manipulation was found in several queries.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays mostly open: only 1992 (Devine and Ostrom materials, N=414) and Smith 1988 are known replications of the order effect; no dated failure found.

source: Sun and Zappala (2025) LLMs as jurors: assessing the potential of LLMs in legal contexts (Law and Human Behavior)
finding: Search summary again reports that GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1 jurors gave higher guilt probabilities than humans (63.56 vs 58.82) yet far fewer guilty verdicts (21% vs 49%). Full text returned HTTP 403.
numbers: 63.56 vs 58.82 probability; 21% vs 49% guilty verdicts (matches earlier claim K14).
limits: Not opened this session. No story-based prompt condition was found, so the question whether a story prompt changes the threshold gap is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 10 stays open on the story-prompt half. Threshold mismatch means a verdict cut-off for our agent must be calibrated separately from its probability estimate.

source: Anchors in the Machine (2025) and Anchored Confabulation (2026) on anchoring in LLMs
finding: Search summaries only: prompt-level fixes largely fail to remove numeric anchoring; one confirmed intermediate fact can raise confident wrong completion of remaining steps.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; search summary only. Anchored Confabulation (2604.25931) is described as having one test only directionally consistent.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: both point to early commitment effects but neither is a coherence-shift test. Treat as pointers.

source: Negative search: LLM studies that vary rival-story count, uniqueness or story-versus-element order
finding: Searches for rival-hypothesis calibration, story-first vs element-first, and coverage-audit token cost returned related work (diverse hypothesis sampling, Solomonoff-inspired ranking 2512.17145, Collaborative Calibration 2404.09127) but no controlled test.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Snippets only. Absence of evidence from a limited number of queries, not proof.
agent_relevance: Gaps 3, 6 (token cost) and 7 stay open and need our own experiment.
